title: What to Have Ready Before a New UK Retailer Issues Your First Order
summary: Most UK retail onboarding delays are preventable. Here is what suppliers who get to first order on time have in common, and what consistently holds others back.
body_markdown:
# What to Have Ready Before a New UK Retailer Issues Your First Order


By[Morgan McKnight](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/morgan-mcknight) , *Integrated Marketing Specialist*


Last Updated November 13, 2026


6 min read


**In this article, learn about:**


- Why the gap between listing confirmation and first order is longer than most suppliers expect


- What UK retailers need from suppliers before the EDI conversation can begin


- Where delays come from and which ones are preventable


- What suppliers who onboard quickly do differently


## The Listing Is Not the Finish Line


Getting a new UK retail listing confirmed is a commercial win. What comes next is an operational one. The two do not happen at the same time, and for many suppliers the gap between them is longer than anticipated.


A buyer agreeing to list a product does not mean the first order can be processed. Before that happens, the retailer needs to issue a Supplier ID, EDI connections need to be established and tested, product master data needs to match what the retailer holds in its system, and the supplier's advance despatch notifications need to be transmitting correctly. Each of those steps has a dependency on the one before it.


For suppliers working with[SPS Commerce](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/fulfillment/) , UK retailer connections are already pre-configured in the network, which shortens the technical setup stage. But the sequencing still matters, and the suppliers who get to first order fastest are those who start the operational work before the commercial conversation is finished.


## What Has to Be in Place Before the Buyer Conversation Starts


Missing product data is the most common source of delay in UK retail onboarding. It stops the EDI setup from starting at all.


UK retailers require GS1-compliant barcodes and accurate product data for every SKU before a listing can be set up in their systems. GTINs need to be registered, and the product hierarchy, packaging dimensions, and unit-of-measure data tied to each GTIN need to match the specification the retailer uses. If that data is incomplete or inconsistent when the buyer relationship is confirmed, the listing setup waits while the supplier corrects it.


Every step in this sequence depends on the one before it. A listing requires a valid GTIN. EDI testing requires an active listing. The Supplier ID arrives only once the listing exists in the retailer's system. Suppliers who arrive at the buyer meeting with GTINs already registered and product data already clean move through every subsequent step faster. For a detailed look at how one major UK retailer structures this process, the[Lidl GB supplier guide](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/what-suppliers-need-to-know-before-working-with-lidl-gb/) covers the full listing and launch sequence from initial contact through to live trading.


## The Supplier ID Is the Starting Gun, Not the Finish Line


Once a listing is confirmed and the retailer has set it up internally, they issue a Supplier ID. This is the trigger for EDI setup to begin. EDI configuration requires the Supplier ID before it can start.


The retailer's test cycle is usually where the most time is spent. Suppliers submit test messages against the retailer's Message Implementation Guide, and the retailer checks them before approving the connection for live trading. This cycle typically runs two to four weeks, with the retailer controlling the pace. What suppliers can control is how quickly they submit accurate test messages on the first pass.


Common reasons first-pass testing fails:


- Document field formats that do not match the retailer's specification


- Quantity and unit-of-measure mismatches between the product data and the DESADV format


- Missing mandatory fields in the ORDRSP or INVOIC that the retailer's system requires


Each failure adds a resubmission cycle. A supplier whose test messages pass on the first attempt goes live two to four weeks sooner than one who takes three rounds of corrections to clear the same test.

## What Getting It Right Looks Like


Suppliers who reach first order on time tend to follow the same sequence, regardless of the retailer.


**1. Register GTINs before approaching any new UK retailer.**


GS1 UK membership and registered barcodes for every SKU in the range are prerequisites. The process can take days to weeks, and listing conversations that start before GTINs are in hand create delays at the first step.


**2. Treat product data as a live document.**


Product data submitted to a retailer at listing needs to stay accurate as packaging, weight, or range composition changes. Data that drifts out of sync with what the retailer holds creates ordering errors long before a buyer notices the problem.


**3. Start EDI preparation before the Supplier ID arrives.**


Connection configuration, field mapping, and internal system integration work can all begin before the retailer issues the Supplier ID. Suppliers who use the post-confirmation waiting period productively cut weeks off the time between listing and live trading.


**4. Validate test documents against the retailer's spec before submitting them.**


The retailer's Message Implementation Guide sets out every field requirement. Running test messages through validation internally before the official test cycle reduces first-pass failure rates and shortens the time to live trading.


**5. Confirm DESADV timing in the test phase.**


Testing transmission timing during the EDI test phase means the first real order processes cleanly, with the DESADV already in the retailer's system before goods arrive at the distribution centre.


## The First Order Builds the Account's Performance History


A new retail account has no history to draw on. The exception records from the first few weeks of trading become the baseline the buyer sees when they review account performance.


Late DESADVs, invoice mismatches, and document format errors that generate chargebacks in the first month create a track record that takes months to improve. Getting those documents right from the start means the account's history works in the supplier's favour when the first range review comes around.


For suppliers managing multiple UK retail connections through[SPS Commerce](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/fulfillment/) , new account connections are added to the same setup that handles existing retail relationships. Document validation runs before anything reaches the retailer's system, so the first order on a new account gets the same level of monitoring as an established one. The account's performance history starts clean.
